query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) coupled with in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) can effectively be used to study high‐temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability in refractory high-entropy alloys. This combined method allows direct monitoring of the weight gain during oxidation and simultaneous identification of phase transitions and the formation of protective oxide scales.
generation.material_initial_state: A dense refractory high-entropy alloy, synthesized via powder metallurgy or spark plasma sintering, with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Heating the material in a controlled oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., flowing air) at high temperatures (around 1000 °C) while continuously monitoring mass change and phase evolution.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure under controlled heating/cooling rates and oxidizing conditions, ensuring real-time TGA and in situ XRD data acquisition.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of protective oxide layers (such as silicides, spinel, or Cr₂O₃-based phases) which modify the mass and structural state of the material.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, TGA tracks the mass gain due to oxygen uptake (reflecting the kinetics of oxidation), while in situ XRD provides phase identification and detects phase transitions or the emergence of new oxide phases. This simultaneous monitoring enables correlation between oxidation kinetics and phase stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: A parabolic mass gain curve that corresponds to the formation of a stable oxide scale will be observed, and in situ XRD will identify the formation of oxidation products and any phase transitions, providing a comprehensive picture of the material’s oxidation behaviour and phase stability.
generation.baseline: At room temperature the material exhibits negligible oxidation and retains its initial phase composition as confirmed by standard XRD.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this method may be limited if the oxidation rate is so high that protective scales spall quickly, or if the experimental setup lacks the resolution to detect minor phase changes during rapid transformations.
generation.uncertainty: While the combined TGA–in situ XRD approach should capture the overall oxidation kinetics and phase evolution, the detection of very subtle phase changes or the exact quantification of minor oxide phases remains instrument-dependent.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of refractory HEA samples and perform high-temperature oxidation tests in a TGA equipped with in situ XRD. For one set, use the combined method to record weight gain and phase changes in real time. In a control set, perform identical oxidation treatments and conduct ex situ XRD and SEM analyses. Compare the real-time data with the post-mortem analyses.
measurements: TGA-derived weight gain vs. time curves
Real-time XRD patterns capturing phase evolution
Ex situ XRD of oxidized samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ XRD and TGA data fail to reveal a parabolic weight gain typical of protective oxide scale formation or if expected oxide phases and phase transitions are not detected during the high-temperature exposure, then the combined TGA–in situ XRD method would be considered unsuitable for studying high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability in these materials.
